title: Candomblé takes root in Salvador, Bahia
summary: Candomblé, created by enslaved Africans and their descendants, emerged around Salvador, Bahia, in the late eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. The Casa Branca terreiro in Engenho Velho da Federação, founded around 1830 on land behind the Barroquinha church, is considered by many the oldest in Brazil and is said to have given rise to the Gantois and Axé Opô Afonjá houses. Iphan listed it as heritage in 1986.

uncertainty.note: The Salvador municipal page calls the founding date an estimate around 1830; Encyclopedia.com says Butler dates the Engenho Velho community to about 1830 and that the religion emerged in the late eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.

as_recorded.value: Engenho Velho community in Bahia, possibly the oldest in Brazil, to about 1830

where.modern_name: Salvador, Bahia, Brazil (Casa Branca, Engenho Velho da Federação)

importance.justification: Marks the rise in Bahia of a religion built by enslaved Africans, with a terreiro now recognised as national heritage.

reviewer_note: Least sure: the 1830 date is an estimate for one terreiro (Casa Branca), used as the anchor for a religion that emerged over the late 18th and 19th centuries; Iphan was not opened directly (the municipal page reports the 1986 listing). The point is Salvador city.
